title: The Original Way
subtitle: A Pilgrim's Guide to the Camino Primitivo
author: CaminoPlus
rights: © 2026 CaminoPlus. All rights reserved. Passages quoted from the classics are in the public domain and are credited where they appear.

spans.t: The Camino Primitivo is the Original Way, and it is the demanding one. It leaves Oviedo, the old capital of Asturias, climbs through slate-roofed mountain villages, crosses into Galicia at a pass of ~1,030 m, passes the Roman walls of Lugo, and at Melide joins the last stretch of the Camino Francés to the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela. It is ~320 km in all.
The promise of this book is simple.
By the last page you will know whether the mountains are your Camino, what each of the fourteen walking days asks of you, and what to check before you leave home.
How to use it

If you are a month or more away, read the next four chapters in order: the Way in brief, whether it suits you, when to go, and what to do before you go. Then read the days by region, and the chapter on the high road, which covers the one big choice on this Camino.
If you are on the road tonight, go straight to your stage. Each day says what the walking is like, what is worth a pause, and where to take care.
If you are only dreaming, start with "Is this Camino for you?" and finish with "The inner Way".
What this book is not

It is not a live map, a timetable or a booking service. It is written from public sources, named at the end, and not from a walk. It names no hostels, cafes or shops, and it gives no prices, opening hours or bed counts. They change from season to season, and a wrong one costs a tired person dearly. For those, use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.
This book was written with AI assistance, from public sources, and its author has not walked the road. So it gives you sources instead of memories, and it says plainly when the sources disagree.
Every distance here carries a tilde,

, because it is approximate. Published lengths differ between sources, and this book says so where it matters. Where something depends on the season (snow, mist, a closed path, heat, a river after rain), it says
check before you go
, and means it. On this road that line matters more than on most.
A few words you will meet
Buen Camino
, "good Way", is what pilgrims and locals say to one another as you pass. An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel. The
credencial
is your pilgrim's passport, a folded card that you carry and have stamped along the way. Each stamp is a
sello
. The
Compostela
is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules, which the chapter on arriving sets out.

In Asturias the official pages give both the Spanish and the Asturian name of a place (Oviedo and Uviéu, Grado and Grau, Tineo and Tinéu); this book uses the Spanish forms there. In Galicia it follows the Galician forms of the Xunta de Galicia, such as O Cádavo and A Fonsagrada.
Carry what you need, ask before you gamble with the weather, and take your time over the long hill.
Buen Camino.
Where it goes

The Camino Primitivo runs from Oviedo, the capital of Asturias, to Santiago de Compostela. The first ~146 km are in Asturias: from the cathedral of Oviedo west through the councils of Las Regueras, Grado, Salas, Tineo, Allande and Grandas de Salime, up to the pass of Puerto del Acebo, which is the regional border. In Galicia the road crosses the province of Lugo, passes through the city of Lugo itself, and at Melide, in the province of A Coruña, joins the Camino Francés. The Xunta de Galicia says the Primitivo converges with the French Way there and continues to the cathedral, ~53 km away.
How long is it?

The app's catalog gives ~320 km. The Confraternity of St James says about the same, and the Asturias tourism pages speak of ~321 km. They count differently. The Asturias itinerary measures ~146 km from Oviedo to the pass (and ~142 km by the high variant called Hospitales, described later). The Xunta measures ~167 km from the pass to Santiago on its route page, and says ~171 km on another page of its own. The Spanish Wikipedia gives ~313 km. The fourteen stages this book follows add up to ~312 km.

Plan on ~320 km and expect a few kilometres either way. Stage counts vary too. Asturias divides its part into seven stages, the Xunta divides the Galician part into eight, and the Spanish Wikipedia says the standard walk takes ten to fifteen days. This book follows fourteen walking days named by their stage towns, and the chapter on the high road shows where others cut them.
Why it is called the original
Primitivo
means first, original. The Xunta calls this the original and oldest pilgrimage route, and Asturias calls it the first Jacobean route recorded in history. The reason is a king.
A short history

The story begins in the early years of the ninth century. Asturias tells it as a legend. Bishop Teodomiro of Iria Flavia, in the far west of the Kingdom of Asturias, came to the court at Oviedo with news: a hermit had seen strange lights over the forest of Libredón, pointing to a tomb where the apostle James was believed to lie. King Alfonso II wanted to see it for himself, and ordered a shrine built on the spot. The Xunta de Galicia says that this king, known as the Chaste, travelled to Santiago in the first third of the ninth century to confirm that the remains were the apostle's, and it calls him the first pilgrim king.

The Asturias pages are frank about what that means for your feet. They say the historical sources are not very reliable and that nothing fixes the exact route the king followed. They suggest, as the logical guess, the Roman road from Lucus Asturum, near Oviedo, to Lucus Augusti, which is Lugo. The Xunta says the Primitivo mainly follows the path of Roman roads. So "the road of Alfonso II" is a tradition and a sensible guess, not a surveyed line.

The Xunta adds that his successor, Alfonso III, took the route twice, and it calls him the architect of the consecration of the second basilica in Santiago in 899. Once León became the capital, the kings of the eleventh and twelfth centuries promoted the Camino Francés. The Primitivo stayed an alternative, for pilgrims who wished to venerate the relics at the cathedral of Oviedo and in Lugo.
The Confraternity of St James records a Spanish saying about Oviedo:
Quien va a Santiago y no al Salvador, visita al criado y deja al Señor

. Whoever goes to Santiago but not to the Saviour visits the servant and leaves the Lord. In its account, many pilgrims left the Francés at León and walked some ~120 km north to the cathedral of Oviedo, then took the Primitivo back to the Francés.
In 2015 UNESCO listed the route as a World Heritage Site, together with the Camino del Norte.
Who walks it now

Wikipedia, reporting the Pilgrim's Office statistics, says about 24,400 pilgrims finished the Primitivo in 2024, making it the fifth most walked route. About 58 per cent of them started in Oviedo, and most finished in August.
What it feels like

Asturias gives a reason why this road has kept its character. The mountains of the south-west are complicated country, and until recently they held back roads and development, so the lands the Way crosses have stayed tied to farming and livestock. You will see it in the slate roofs, the dry-stone walls, and the raised granaries called
hórreos
. Asturias says those who know the Jacobean routes well call the Primitivo the one that has best kept the essence of the old pilgrimage.

The walking follows the arc of the map: hills and farmland first, then high mountain days with few villages, then Galicia, with Roman Lugo, Romanesque churches, and from Melide the last stretch of the Francés. It is not an easy arc. The next chapter says so plainly.
The honest answer: it is demanding

The Primitivo has a name for being hard, and the sources agree. The Confraternity of St James calls it a hard route through the mountains, with a great deal of climbing and descending, though mainly on well-made paths, and with a fair amount of road walking. It adds that you should really have some other hill-walking experience before going this way. The app's catalog rates the route 4 on its scale of 1 to 5. It rates the Camino Francés 3 and the Camino Inglés 2.

The hard part is the first half. The official Asturias pages list ~600 m of climbing in ~8 km on the way to the Alto del Palo, and ~600 m in ~13 km up to the pass of Puerto del Acebo. They also describe long days: ~26 km on the first, ~28 km on the fourth. Across the border, the Xunta de Galicia rates none of its Galician stages above medium; the two it rates highest are San Romao da Retorta to Melide and the last day into Santiago. No official source gives a total ascent for the whole route, so this book gives none.

There is one more thing to weigh. The weather in these hills is a risk, not a detail. The Confraternity says it can be harsh even in summer, damp and cold, and can change very quickly. The chapter on body, weather and safety says what to do about it.
Who it suits

items.t: Walkers with some hill experience
, or a long training build-up behind them, who are comfortable with climbs of several hundred metres and a few days over ~25 km.
Pilgrims who want a quieter road.
Wikipedia calls the Primitivo a popular alternative to the much more heavily travelled Camino Francés. Remember that the last ~53 km, from Melide, are the Francés.
People who like mountains for their own sake
: slate-roofed villages, dry-stone walls, a reservoir far below you, and days when the road crosses empty country.
Walkers who can plan.
The official pages describe some days as passing hardly any villages, so you will carry food and water, and you will want to know where you are sleeping before you start the long ones.

spans.t: Who should think twice

items.t: If you have never walked several long days in a row, train first, or choose a gentler Way. The Camino Inglés (~120 km) has its own book in this series, and so does the Camino Francés.
If you have a knee, hip or heart condition, ask a doctor before you commit to the climbs and descents.
If your dates fall in winter, read "When to go" carefully. Snow and mist on the high sections change what is sensible.
If you hate wet feet, accept that Asturias and Galicia are green for a reason.

spans.t: None of this is a reason to be afraid. It is a reason to prepare, and many people do: about 24,400 finished the Primitivo in 2024.
If the mountains are too much

You do not have to choose between the whole road and nothing. The high road over the Hospitales is optional: the lower road is the official one, and the chapter on the two roads explains the choice. You can also split the stages into shorter days: the Asturias pages say their seven stages can be subdivided as often as you like. And you can start later along the Way. About a third of the pilgrims who finished in 2024 started in Lugo, Wikipedia reports. If you start anywhere other than Oviedo, read the Pilgrim's Office rules for the Compostela, set out in the chapter on arriving, and ask the Office.
The Primitivo asks a lot of the body. Go at a pace that still lets you look up.
Patterns, not forecasts

This chapter gives patterns, not forecasts, and the patterns come with a warning: the figures below are for three towns, and the Primitivo spends several days well above any of them. Oviedo's weather station sits at ~336 m and Lugo's at ~445 m. The pass into Galicia is ~1,030 m, according to the Xunta de Galicia, and A Fonsagrada, the first Galician town, stands at ~965 m, according to Wikipedia. Expect it to be colder up there. The Confraternity of St James says the weather in these hills can be harsh even in summer, damp and cold, and can change very quickly.
The rain
All three places have an oceanic climate: mild, green and wet. Wikipedia's climate tables for the period 1991 to 2020 give roughly this:

items.t: Oviedo:
~1,030 mm of rain a year. The driest month is July (~44 mm) and the wettest November (~134 mm).
Lugo:
~1,140 mm a year. July is the driest (~33 mm) and November the wettest (~154 mm).
Santiago:
~1,500 mm a year, and the article's own text says about ~1,800. July is the driest (~31 mm) and October the wettest (~214 mm).

spans.t: So the shape is the same everywhere. July is the driest month, with June and August close behind, and the heavy rain runs from October to January. None of these months is guaranteed dry. Carry rain gear in every season.
Warm months

In Oviedo the average afternoon high is ~24 °C in August, in Lugo ~25 °C, and in Santiago ~25 °C in July and August. That is an average. The same tables record extremes of ~41 °C at both Oviedo and Lugo in the past, and the safety chapter has a section on heat. Wikipedia reports that most pilgrims finish the Primitivo in August, and the Confraternity calls the route very popular in July and August. In a busy month, work out where you will sleep before you set out each day, and use the app and local information to see what is open.
Spring and autumn

Spring and autumn sit between the extremes, with the added risk of the wettest months. Oviedo's average afternoon high is ~19 °C in September and ~14 °C in November, and its rain roughly triples between July and November. Lugo's April high is ~17 °C, and its record lows go below freezing from October to May. Take layers, a proper waterproof, and a day you can lose to the weather.
Winter

Winter is the hardest case, and the high ground is the reason. The Xunta says the pass is covered in snow in the harsh seasons. In Oviedo's table the average January high is ~12 °C and the record low about −6 °C, and Lugo's average January high is ~11 °C with a low of ~2 °C and a record of about −12 °C. Oviedo's station counts about four snowy days a year, at ~336 m. The pass is ~700 m higher.

The days are short as well. For Oviedo and Lugo, a standard solar calculation gives ~9 hours of daylight at the December solstice, with sunrise near nine in the morning, and ~15 hours at the June solstice, with sunset after ten at night. Do not plan to walk in the dark.

Before you set out in winter, ask locally and read current notices. The Confraternity's advice, if you are contemplating the high-level variant, is to restrict yourself to the summer months. The Asturias tourism pages give no closing date for that variant and no weather rule for it. This book will not guess one.
Check before you go.
A Holy Year

2027 is a Jacobean Holy Year, a year in which 25 July falls on a Sunday; the next is 2032. The cathedral's Holy Door is opened only in Holy Years, and the Pilgrim's Office reports that 272,703 pilgrims received the Compostela in the Holy Year of 2010. If you plan to walk in 2027, arrange your beds earlier than usual.
Choosing a month

The driest weather and the longest evenings are in June to September, and so are the crowds of July and August. The shoulder months are quieter and wetter, and ask for extra layers and flexible days. Winter asks for mountain skills, not just boots. Whichever month you choose, look at the forecast of the Spanish weather agency, AEMET, for the high ground before every mountain day.
Your credencial

The credencial is your pilgrim's passport. The Pilgrim's Office in Santiago describes the official model as a card of sixteen concertina-folded pages, with boxes for the stamps you collect on the way. You can get it in person at the Office, or from institutions the cathedral has authorised: parish churches, associations of friends of the Way, pilgrim hostels and confraternities, in Spain and abroad. Some associations are authorised to issue their own. The Office also describes a digital credential, an app for Android and iOS.

The Office gives the credencial two practical purposes: access to the hostels of the Way, and proof when you ask for the Compostela. It also says the credencial "does not generate any rights". Stamps are usually collected where you sleep, and also in parish churches, monasteries, cathedrals, hotels, town halls and other places. Get yours before you start walking, and keep it dry.
Getting to Oviedo, and home from Santiago

Wikipedia says Oviedo has a railway station with long-distance, regional and suburban services, and that the city is served by Asturias Airport, ~48 km away, linked to Oviedo by motorway and a scheduled bus. Santiago's airport, according to Wikipedia, lies ~12 km east of the city and has flights to Spanish and European cities. Timetables and routes change, so check them close to your date, and book your way home before you go: it is easier to plan with a clear head than at the end of the road.

If you would rather not carry your pack, the Asturias tourism pages list luggage-transport services that move bags from one lodging to the next. Ask which of them cover your days; the pages carry the current names and terms.
Training

Asturias advises starting to walk a few months before you go, in comfortable footwear that is already broken in. The climbs matter here, so train on hills, and walk several days in a row with the pack you will carry. Practise the long days, not only the short ones. If you cannot do ~20 km on tired legs at home, the mountains will tell you so.

Surfaces change a lot. The official stage pages describe the first day as mostly on tarmac roads, the fourth and fifth as mostly on dirt and gravel tracks, and the sixth as about half tarmac. Choose shoes that suit both, and test them for a long day before you leave.
Packing

The Asturias tourism pages recommend a rucksack that does not weigh more than ten kilos. They list sun cream, a waterproof jacket, a basic first-aid kit, comfortable broken-in footwear, sandals or flip-flops for the evening, and a torch or head torch. They also name a walking stick among the essential items. For this road add what the weather asks for:

items.t: Layers.
A warm layer, a hat and light gloves. The Confraternity warns that these hills can be damp and cold even in summer.
A real waterproof
, and a way to keep one dry set of clothes dry.
Poles
, if you use them, for the long descents.
Food and water for the days that pass few villages.
The official page calls the fifth stage extremely natural and the sixth one that hardly passes through any towns.
Your maps, saved before you go.
Mountain signal can fail. The Confraternity says the waymarking is good overall, and also that you can be shrouded in mist for a whole day.

spans.t: Weigh the pack before you leave. Everything you add is carried up the climbs of ~600 m.
Money and paperwork
Carry some cash for small villages, and a card for the bigger towns. Keep your passport or identity card with your credencial. Check the cover on your health insurance, and make a note of
, the European emergency number.
Language

Spanish will serve you in both regions. In Asturias it is the only official language, though Asturian is also spoken and protected by law, and the official pages give place names in both. In Galicia, Galician and Spanish are both official languages, and the Xunta's pages use the Galician names. A few words go a long way:
buenos días
gracias
¿dónde está...?
and
Buen Camino
What to decide before you leave

items.t: The high road or the low road.
Decide the rule you will use on the day, not the answer: the chapter on the two roads gives it.
How many days.
This book follows fourteen. Add a rest day in Lugo, or two short days in the mountains, if you are unsure.
Where you will sleep on the days that pass few villages.
Look in the app and ask locally, and book if you are walking in a busy month.

chapters.title: Asturias: Oviedo to Grandas de Salime

spans.t: The character of these days

The first six days belong to Asturias. You leave a capital, cross farmland and low hills, and then climb into the mountains of the south-west, where villages are small, roofs are slate, and the Way spends hours on dirt and gravel tracks. The first four days run ~26 km, ~22 km, ~19 km and ~28 km, and then come two days of real mountain walking (~17 km, ~20 km).

The distances in this chapter come from the official Asturias tourism pages, which divide this part of the road into seven stages. Their seventh stage, from Grandas de Salime to the pass, begins the next chapter. Other sources give slightly different figures, as "The Way in brief" says.
Day 1: Oviedo to Grado (~26 km)

The Way begins at the gates of the cathedral. The official pages describe it as a Gothic church with its Holy Chamber, the pre-Romanesque palatine chapel of Alfonso II, and a Romanesque carving of the Saviour on the south side of the transept, in front of which, they say, many pilgrims consider their journey to have begun. The cathedral and the Holy Chamber are on the UNESCO list.

You leave by the nineteenth-century streets, pass the old Provincial Hospice, and then the city is behind you. The pages call the day a route without major difficulties: the foothills of Mount Naranco, a steep descent between Llampaxuga and Lloriana, a climb to Taraniellu, a descent to Premoñu, and then a flat run into Grado. Most of it is on tarmac roads, so watch the traffic. In the villages look for the
hórreos
and
paneras

, the raised granaries, which are particularly plentiful at Peñaflor, and for small chapels such as those at Llampaxuga and Lloriana. The pages also point to the Roman baths of Santa Eulalia de Valdunu.

The road was a pilgrim road long ago. The official pages mention a hospital of San Juan founded in Oviedo in 1096, a few metres from the cathedral, and a hostel at L'Escampleru from the fourteenth century. In Grado they single out the chapel of Los Dolores, plain outside and richly Baroque within, and the Valdecarzana palace.
Day 2: Grado to Salas (~22 km)

The first job of the day is the climb to the Fresno pass: ~300 m in ~4.5 km, steeper in the last stretch before the top. Then you drop to the River Narcea at Cornellana, and climb again, much more gently, to Salas.

Cornellana is the day's great stop. The monastery of San Salvador mixes Romanesque and Baroque, was one of the most important monasteries in the north of the peninsula according to the official pages, and is one of the sites UNESCO added to the list in 2015. The pages also place the battle of the Casas del Puente nearby, where Ramiro I won the throne of Oviedo from Nepociano. In Salas, the Gothic collegiate church of Santa María la Mayor holds the mausoleum of Fernando de Valdés, the inquisitor who founded the University of Oviedo. Most of the day is on asphalt or concrete, with about a third on dirt and gravel.
Day 3: Salas to Tineo (~19 km)

An easier day, and a good one to listen to your legs. The climb is gradual, steeper at the start between Salas and Porciles, and then the profile settles. The surfaces are evenly mixed: tarmac verges, dirt and gravel.

Look at the roofs. The official pages say that as you pass from Salas into Tineo, slate slabs gradually replace tiles. They also note a pilgrims' establishment at La Espina documented as early as 883, which they call one of the oldest in the Jacobean world. (Another of their pages gives the same year, 883, for a hospital at Bourres. Sources are not tidy about the first hospital.)

Tineo was important on the road. The pages say King Alfonso IX ordered pilgrims to pass through it in 1222, and that its pilgrims' hospital is documented from the thirteenth century and stood until the nineteenth. This is also where you decide about tomorrow. Read "The high road and other ways to split the days" before you reach Tineo, and decide with the forecast in your hand.
Day 4: Tineo to Pola de Allande (~28 km)

This is the official itinerary, and it is the lower road. It is long, and the official pages say it runs mostly on dirt and gravel tracks. You climb ~200 m in ~5 km to the Piedratecha pass, drop ~300 m in ~3 km, and then make a last climb at the border of Tineo and Allande, to Lavadoira, before the descent into Pola de Allande.

In between is slate country: small farming villages such as Vil.lal.luz, Vega del Rey, Campiel.lu and Bourres, meadows, woods and dry-stone walls. A short detour from the route, ~400 m according to one official page, leads to the monastery of Santa María la Real de Obona. In 1222 Alfonso IX ordered that it be an obligatory stop for pilgrims. At the end, the Cienfuegos palace stands on its hill above Pola de Allande, an example of rural Baroque.

The alternative, the high Hospitales road, leaves this route in the hills after Bourres. It does not pass Pola de Allande at all. If you take it, Asturias advises sleeping at Campiello or Bourres the night before.
Day 5: Pola de Allande to Berducedo (~17 km)

A short day that the official pages call intense. For ~8 km you climb ~600 m to the Alto del Palo, through a natural setting of dense vegetation, streams and dry-stone walls, some of which hold back boulders that look ready to tumble onto the Way. The pages call it one of the most beautiful routes of the Asturian Jacobean roads. Almost all of it is dirt and gravel, and until you pass the summit only a few isolated farmhouses mark the way. Carry food and water for the whole climb.

At the top are the remains of the Roman reservoir that gave the pass its name, and a tale that witches held the last documented coven in Asturias there. After a sharp first descent the going is gentler, through Montefurado, Lago and Berducedo. Montefurado owes its name, says Asturias, to the gold mines the Romans opened, and the churches of Lago and Berducedo are flanked by centuries-old yew trees. This is where the Hospitales road rejoins, ~8 km before Berducedo.
Day 6: Berducedo to Grandas de Salime (~20 km)

This is the day of the reservoir. You pass A Mesa and Buspol, where, the pages say, one of the oldest bells in the region is kept, then enter the pine plantations above the Salime reservoir. The views are the day's reward. Then comes the descent of ~8 km, in places very steep, which the official pages say was famous in the Middle Ages for its danger. The old village and bridge of Salime lie under the water. You cross the dam, which hides a mural by Joaquín Vaquero Turcios.

After the water comes a climb of more than ~5 km to Grandas de Salime, most of it along the shoulder of the AS-14 road. Take care here: walk facing the traffic, keep well to the edge, and do not walk this stretch in poor light. The collegiate church of San Salvador stands at the end. The Spanish Wikipedia adds that in 1222 Alfonso IX obliged pilgrims to pass through Grandas as well. The stage hardly passes through any villages, so carry what you need.

chapters.title: The border and the high Lugo hills

spans.t: The character of these days

Three long days take you over the border and across the high ground of the province of Lugo. You climb to a pass of ~1,030 m, walk through hill country of small hamlets and medieval hospital sites, and descend at last to the Roman walls of Lugo. The days are long (~25 km, ~25 km, ~30 km), the country is open, and the weather on the first of them is the weather of the mountains.

From here the figures come from the Xunta de Galicia's route pages, which describe only the Galician part of the Way, from the pass to Santiago, in eight stages with their own stage towns. This book's days add up the Xunta's sections to reach the usual stage towns, so their lengths are sums, good to a kilometre or two.
Day 7: Grandas de Salime to A Fonsagrada (~25 km)

The day begins with a climb that the official Asturias pages call continuous, straight and not very steep, except for the last push to the top. It is ~13 km, rising ~600 m. Most of it is on dirt and gravel tracks, through the villages of Cereixeira, Castro, Xestoselo and Penafonte, and between them the path often runs through tunnels of vegetation. At Castro, the large archaeological site of Chao Samartín preserves pre-Roman dwellings and the ruins of a Roman mansion; the pages say it was declared an Asset of Cultural Interest in 2014 and has a modern interpretation centre.

The pass is the border. Asturias calls it Puerto del Acebo, and the Xunta calls it Alto do Acevo and gives its height as ~1,030 m. The Xunta says it is a lovely spot, covered in snow in the harsh seasons and lush in the milder months. In winter,
check before you go
: ask locally about snow and mist before you start this climb.

On the Galician side the first goal is Fonfría and its freshwater spring. Between Fonfría and Paradanova the Xunta places a major pilgrims' hospital, on land held by San Xoán de Paradanova, which it says was still working at the start of the twentieth century. At Paradanova the Xunta marks two options: one runs through the centre of A Fonsagrada, past a holy fountain linked by tradition to a miracle attributed to St James, and the other goes by A Proba de Burón. The Xunta measures the first at ~167 km for the whole Galician Way and the second at ~168 km. Both meet again at Montouto. The Spanish Wikipedia says the Burón route was the main one until the eighteenth century. A Fonsagrada, according to Wikipedia, stands at ~965 m.
Day 8: A Fonsagrada to O Cádavo (~25 km)

The Xunta rates this stretch low to medium-low. It stays high, from ~965 m at A Fonsagrada to ~710 m at O Cádavo. From A Fonsagrada you pass San Xoán do Padrón and reach Hospital de Montouto, where the two options come together. A half-ruined hospital stands there, which Wikipedia calls the New Royal Hospital of Santiago de Montouto, with roots in an older royal hospital founded, it says, by Pedro I, "the Cruel". The Xunta's page shows a dolmen at the site, and the Confraternity of St James lists the old hospital and the dolmen among the things worth seeing.
Then Paradavella, which the Xunta says is noted for its
pallozas

, the primitive rural dwellings. Beyond it the path alternates between dense forest and open land near the C-630 road, so take care near the traffic. It passes A Degolada, where you enter the municipality of Baleira, then climbs to the Alto de A Vaqueriza at ~840 m. Near A Fontaneira, the Xunta records a tradition that the Campo da Matanza was the site of a clash between Alfonso II and a Muslim army. At O Cádavo, ~710 m up, you are in the capital of Baleira, which the Xunta calls the second most important town after A Fonsagrada on the Primitive Route in Galicia.
Day 9: O Cádavo to Lugo (~30 km)

By this book's figures this is the longest day of the whole walk. The Xunta's own stage, from Paradavella, ends at Castroverde, ~7.5 km beyond O Cádavo, and its next stage runs from Castroverde to Lugo, ~22 km. Walking both in one go makes ~30 km. If it is too much, Castroverde gives you a place to stop, and the walk to Lugo becomes a ~22 km day the morning after.

From O Cádavo you pass Vilalle. Close by, on a complementary route, is Vilabade, where the church of Santa María, a National Monument built in the middle of the fifteenth century as a Franciscan convent church, holds a Baroque altarpiece of 1759. Castroverde, at ~540 m, has an old castle keep high above the town, a reminder, says the Xunta, of the houses of Lemos and Altamira.

Beyond it the path reaches Soutomerille, an abandoned village with a pre-Romanesque church of San Salvador and a stone lattice window from the time of Alfonso III, in the ninth or tenth century. At Gondar you cross the River Romeán and enter the municipality of Lugo, then pass Carballido, and Lugo comes into view.

Lugo is worth a day. Wikipedia says its Roman walls, a circuit of ~2,117 m with 71 towers and ten gates, are from the third century, are the only completely intact Roman walls in the world, and have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000. The walk along the top is continuous. The cathedral dates from around 1129, and the Xunta says it holds a papal privilege to display the Holy Sacrament around the clock. After ~30 km a rest day here is not an indulgence.
The character of these days

The last five days change character half-way. The first two cross the country between Lugo and Melide: Roman roads, Romanesque churches, small villages, and the Careón hills on the border of the provinces of Lugo and A Coruña. At Melide the Primitivo meets the Camino Francés, and the last three days are on the shared road, ~53 km to the cathedral by the Xunta's count.
The distances here are the Xunta de Galicia's stage lengths, from Lugo on. The Xunta rates them low, medium, low, low and medium. The longest, to Melide, is ~28 km.
Day 10: Lugo to San Romao da Retorta (~19 km)

You leave the city through the Roman walls, either by the Porta Miñá (also called the Porta do Carme) or by the Porta de Santiago, in front of the cathedral's neoclassical façade. The Xunta says the path follows the track of a hidden Roman road to the River Miño, which you cross by a bridge that is also of Roman origin. After that you leave the river behind, and from San Vicente do Burgo the Xunta promises striking views of the city receding.

The Xunta calls a detour to the temple of Santalla de Bóveda well worth taking. It is a late Roman structure of the fourth century, listed as a national monument in 1931. The Xunta says the Roman road from Braga to Lugo passed beside it. Back on the Way you reach Bacurín, with its Romanesque church of San Miguel, and the village of O Francés, also known as Hospital. San Vicente do Burgo, ~10 km from Lugo, once had a pilgrims' hospital. The day ends in San Romao da Retorta, in the municipality of Guntín, where a Roman milestone stands outside the Romanesque church. The Xunta calls it evidence that the Primitivo follows the path of an ancient road.
Day 11: San Romao da Retorta to Melide (~28 km)
This is the longest Galician day, and the Xunta rates it medium, with an estimate of about seven hours. Carry lunch, and an early start is wise.

The first ~12 km take you through small villages (O Burgo, Vilacapide, Pacio, Mosteiro and Ferreira) past the Romanesque church of Santa Cruz da Retorta with its stone cross, and across the medieval Ferreira bridge. By the Spanish Wikipedia's kilometre table the bridge is ~10 km beyond San Romao, so it is one place to break the day. Near the end of that stretch is Augas Santas, whose curative springs and ninth-century monastery are described by the Xunta, and the Romanesque church of San Salvador de Merlán.

The next ~8.5 km climb into the Careón mountains, which span the border of Lugo and A Coruña. The Xunta calls the area one of great ecological value, and gives the highest peak, O Careón, as ~798 m. You then cross into the municipality of Toques and pass Vilouriz. Just off the Way is the eleventh-century Romanesque church of Santo Antoniño de Toques, which the Xunta says reuses capitals and pieces from the Visigothic period.

At Melide the road changes. The Xunta says the Primitive Route converges there with the French Route, at the historic town, and continues to Santiago Cathedral ~53 km away. Wikipedia gives the town an elevation of ~456 m.
Day 12: Melide to Arzúa (~15 km)

The first day on the shared road is a short one. The Xunta lists the same stage, with the same length, for both the Primitive and the French Ways, and rates it low. It describes the surface as earth and stone with small asphalt sections between villages, and gradual climbs and descents alternating with flat stretches.

At Boente you will see a fountain with four pipes and a Calvary, across the main road from the church. At Ribadiso you cross the River Iso on a bridge. Arzúa, the Xunta says, is the land of cheese par excellence, and Wikipedia adds that Arzúa-Ulloa cheese has Protected Designation of Origin status. Wikipedia also says that the Camino del Norte meets the Francés at Arzúa. That road has its own book in this series.
Day 13: Arzúa to Arca (~18 km)

Meadows, oaks and eucalyptus surround hamlets with Jacobean names: A Calzada, A Calle, Ferreiros, A Salceda, A Brea, Santa Irene. The land is practically flat. The one thing to watch is the road. The Xunta warns that the path crosses the N-547 highway several times, and asks you to pay special attention to the vehicles.
You arrive at Arca, capital of the municipality of O Pino, the last municipality before Santiago. O Pedrouzo is the main village of the parish of Arca.
Day 14: Arca to Santiago (~20 km)

The last day is rated medium by the Xunta, with an estimate of a little over five hours. You climb from Santo Antón into the municipality of Santiago, and pass O Amenal, Cimadevila and San Paio. At Lavacolla, near the airport, the Xunta says pilgrims once washed in the stream before arriving.

Monte do Gozo, ~380 m high, is where pilgrims first saw the distant cathedral. The Xunta says that by custom the first to reach the top was proclaimed king of the pilgrimage. A ~5 km descent remains. You enter the city by the San Lázaro neighbourhood, the Rúa de San Pedro and the Porta do Camiño, then go through pedestrian streets and squares (Casas Reais, Plaza de Cervantes, Acibechería) to the basilica. In Holy Years the Xunta says the alternative access is the Holy Door at A Quintana.
The next chapter shows other ways to split the road. The chapter on arriving says what to do when you get there.

chapters.title: The high road, and other ways to split the days

spans.t: Two roads over the same mountains

At Tineo the Primitivo offers a choice. The official itinerary goes by Pola de Allande, over the Alto del Palo, to Berducedo. The other way is the Hospitales variant, a high route through the Fonfaraón range, which rejoins at Montefurado, ~8 km before Berducedo. This is the one big decision of the Camino. Read it before you reach Tineo.
What the official pages say

The Asturias tourism pages are the source here. They say the Hospitales section takes its name from the ruins of the pilgrims' establishments preserved there, and that it is believed to have been part of the original route. They also say its extreme hardship, with very steep slopes crossing completely unpopulated land, led pilgrims gradually to choose Pola de Allande instead. They say those who follow it will enjoy magnificent surroundings, "although it is essential to be in good physical shape". They advise sleeping at Campiello or Bourres the night before.

Their numbers are these. The Asturian part is ~146 km by the official route and ~142 km by Hospitales, so the high road is ~4 to ~5 km shorter, depending on whether you read the web page or the brochure. The variant is described in two parts: Salas to Bourres, ~32 km on one page and ~36 km in the official brochure, and Bourres to Berducedo, ~24 km. Taking away the ~19 km from Salas to Tineo, that leaves ~13 to ~16 km on the first day and ~24 km on the second. In the hills, the pages count a climb of more than ~500 m between La Mortera and the top, beside the ruins of the Fonfaraón hospital. They add that the path is a very logical natural line which avoids steep slopes except in a few stretches, with long almost level sections. Along it are the ruins of the old pilgrim hospitals of Paradiella, Valparaíso, Fonfaraón and La Freita, and the great Roman mine cut of La Freita.
The lower road has its own ~600 m climb to the Alto del Palo, in ~8 km, on the day from Pola de Allande. It is not the easy option. It is the sheltered one.
What other sources add

The Spanish Wikipedia calls the Hospitales variant the oldest and most natural line, and says it saves some kilometres and avoids descending to Pola de Allande and climbing the hard Puerto del Palo. In exchange, it says, it crosses the beautiful but inhospitable Sierra de Fonfaraón, without villages and largely above ~1,100 m. It adds that the route is dangerous in winter or in bad weather, which is why the main route went down to the valley.

The Confraternity of St James warns that the weather in these hills can change very quickly and that you can be shrouded in damp mist for a whole day. Its advice is to have hill-walking experience, and to restrict yourself to the summer months if you are contemplating the high-level option. Its page names the Hospitales route as the alternative to Pola de Allande.
What this book does not know

The official Asturias pages used for this book give no closing date and no weather rule for the high road. This book does not guess one. If there is a closure, a notice or a warning, it will be local and current.
Check before you go.
A rule for the day
Decide on the day, at Tineo or on the way to Campiello and Bourres, not weeks ahead.

items.t: Look at the forecast for the high ground, and at the cloud on the hills.
Choose the lower road if the forecast promises rain, mist, snow or strong wind, if the days before were stormy, if you are tired or unwell, or if you have never walked on mountains.
Choose the lower road if you start late. There is no village on the high road to stop in.
If you take the high road, carry food and water for the whole day, warm layers, a saved map, and tell someone your plan. Turn back if the mist closes in.

spans.t: Other ways to split the days
This book follows fourteen walking days. They are not the only plan. The Spanish Wikipedia says the standard walk takes ten to fifteen days.

items.t: In Asturias.

The official pages divide the road to the pass into seven stages: Oviedo to Grado (~26 km), Grado to Salas (~22 km), Salas to Tineo (~19 km), Tineo to Pola de Allande (~28 km), Pola de Allande to Berducedo (~17 km), Berducedo to Grandas de Salime (~20 km) and Grandas de Salime to the pass (~13 km). They say each can be subdivided as often as you like.
In Galicia.

The Xunta de Galicia divides its part into eight stages: Alto do Acevo to Paradavella (~25 km), Paradavella to Castroverde (~20 km), Castroverde to Lugo (~22 km), Lugo to San Romao da Retorta (~19 km), San Romao da Retorta to Melide (~28 km), Melide to Arzúa (~15 km), Arzúa to Arca (~18 km) and Arca to Santiago (~20 km).
Shorter days.
The day to Lugo can break at Castroverde, and the day to Melide at the bridge of Ferreira.

spans.t: Which towns have a hostel, and which are open this month, changes from season to season, so this book lists none. The Asturias pages say there is enough lodging to let you stop when your feet tire. Use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.
Albergue life
An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel: a dormitory with bunk beds, a shared bathroom and often a place to wash your clothes. You show your credencial at the door, and the host, the
hospitalero

, stamps it and tells you the house rules. The Pilgrim's Office lists access to "hostels offered by the Christian hospitality of the Way" as the first practical use of the credencial. It also notes that hostels without subsidies are kept going by what pilgrims contribute. Leave a place cleaner than you found it, and give what you can.

The Asturias tourism pages say that along their part of the road there are public hostels, private ones, and a variety of other lodging such as hotels and guesthouses. How each one works, whether you can book it, and whether it is open this month, changes, so ask, and call ahead on the days that pass few villages.
The etiquette of a dormitory is short and kind.

items.t: Arrive, claim a bed, shower, wash and hang out your clothes. The evening is for resting.
Keep your voice low after the lights go out, and do not rustle bags at night or before dawn. Pack your rucksack in the hall.
Use a head torch, not the main light. Silence your phone.
Keep your pack and shoes off the bed, and your boots where the house puts them. Wet boots take time to dry in these hills.
Earplugs are a small comfort that goes a long way. Somebody will snore, and if it is you, apologise at breakfast.
Keep your valuables close.

spans.t: Bedbugs

can be a risk in any shared bed anywhere. Check the seams of the mattress, keep your pack and clothes off the bed, and if you find bites, tell the host and wash and dry everything hot. It is not a reason to avoid hostels, only a reason to look before you lie down.
If you are ill, tired or sleeping badly, take a private room. It is not cheating. After a mountain day, a good night is part of the walk.
Eating
Many places along the Way offer a
menú del peregrino
, a set meal for pilgrims. Ask what is on it, and what it costs, before you sit. A set meal is a good way to eat well on a long day, and an easy way to try what the region cooks.
Asturias calls its cuisine one of the region's great attractions. The tourism pages name
fabada
, a white-bean stew, as an emblematic dish, and natural cider as an iconic drink. The cider festival, the
espicha
, is one of the most common festivities on the Asturian calendar. In Galicia look for
polbo á feira

, the fair-style octopus, which Wikipedia calls a traditional Galician dish and the totemic food of the festivities of Lugo's patron saint. Near Arzúa there is cheese: Arzúa-Ulloa has Protected Designation of Origin. At the end of the road is the
tarta de Santiago
, the almond cake, which Wikipedia says has its origin in the Middle Ages and the Camino.
You do not need to eat all of it. Pick one local thing a day.
Food and water in the mountains

The official pages describe the day from Pola de Allande as having only a few isolated farmhouses before the Alto del Palo, and the day to Grandas de Salime as hardly passing through any villages. On the Hospitales road there are no villages at all. On any such day, fill your bottles at the last village and carry more than you think you need. Carry lunch and something for the evening as well, because a small village's shop or cafe may be closed when you arrive. Do not drink from a stream or trough unless you know it is meant for people, and if a fountain is marked as unsuitable, believe the sign.
Resting
The Primitivo is not a road to rush. A day of rest is part of the walk, and the road offers good places for it.

items.t: Oviedo

, before you start. The Confraternity of St James lists the cathedral, the Holy Chamber, and three pre-Romanesque churches on the edge of the city: San Julián de los Prados, Santa María del Naranco and San Miguel de Lillo.
Lugo
, after the long day over the hills. The Roman walls can be walked in an afternoon.
Santiago
, at the end. It deserves more than a night, and the chapter on arriving says why.

spans.t: On the road, listen to your body before you listen to your plan. Take short days as short days. If something hurts in a way that grows rather than fades, stop, rest, and let a doctor look at it. You are not walking to prove anything.

This chapter is plain on purpose, and it asks for more care than usual, because the Primitivo has real mountain days and the weather can turn quickly. Nothing here is a reason to stay at home. It is what a careful walker does.
Feet and legs

Your feet decide how the walk goes. Stop at the first hot spot and dress it, before it becomes a blister. Change your socks at lunch if they are damp. Rest for a few minutes each hour, and eat and drink before you are hungry or thirsty.

The descents are as demanding as the climbs. The official pages describe a drop of ~300 m in ~3 km on the day to Pola de Allande and a long descent of ~8 km, in places very steep, on the day to Grandas de Salime. Shorten your stride and use poles if you have them. If you feel a sharp or growing pain in a knee, a shin or the top of a foot, stop. Rest it for a day, or take a shorter stage. A day lost to rest is better than a week lost to an injury.
Mountain weather

The Confraternity of St James says the weather here can be harsh, even in summer, damp and cold, and can change very quickly. The Xunta de Galicia says the pass into Galicia is covered in snow in the harsh seasons. Take both seriously.

items.t: Look at the forecast the evening before and again in the morning.
AEMET, the Spanish state weather agency, publishes forecasts. Look at the high ground, not only the town you are leaving.
Start early on mountain days,
so that a slow climb or a wrong turn does not leave you on a ridge at dusk.
Wet clothes cool you quickly,
even in mild weather. Carry a waterproof, a warm layer, a hat and gloves, and keep one dry layer in a bag that cannot get wet. If you start to shiver, stop and get warm before you go on.
In mist, stay on the marked way.
The Confraternity says the waymarking is good overall, but if you cannot see the next marker, stop, and do not guess. Go back to the last one you saw. If you have a saved map, use it.
If a day looks wrong, change the plan.
Take the lower road, stop early, or wait a day. The chapter on the two roads gives a rule for the Hospitales.

spans.t: Paths, steps and old stones are slippery in the wet. After heavy rain, ask locally about flooded sections.
Heat

Wikipedia's climate tables show averages of ~24 to ~25 °C in the warmest months, and past extremes of ~41 °C in both Oviedo and Lugo. On a hot day, start early, wear a hat, put on sun cream, and carry more water than you think you need. Rest in the shade through the hottest hours. A headache, dizziness or nausea in the heat are signs to stop, get into the shade, and drink. If they do not pass, ask for help. In dry summers, ask locally about fires and closed paths.
Roads, paths and dogs

Much of the Primitivo is on tracks and paths, and much of it is not. The official pages describe the first day as mostly on tarmac roads. On the day to Grandas de Salime, the climb of more than ~5 km runs mostly along the shoulder of the AS-14 road. Between Paradavella and O Cádavo the path runs near the C-630, and on the way to Arca it crosses the N-547 several times. The Xunta asks you to pay special attention to vehicles.
Wherever you must walk on a road, face the oncoming traffic, keep well to the edge, and wear something bright. Never walk on a road in the dark or in thick mist.
Dogs on farms may bark as you pass. Walk on calmly and do not stare or run.
Staying safe on your own

Tell someone where you plan to sleep each night, and message them when you arrive. Keep your phone charged, carry your map saved on it, and know the name of the last village you passed. Mountain signal can fail, so do not rely on it.
When to stop

Stop, and get help, for chest pain, a fever, severe dizziness, a fall with a blow to the head, a swollen joint, or anything that frightens you. Stop too if you are cold and cannot get warm, if you are lost in mist, or if you have run out of water. A doctor is the right person for a worry, and a plan can always change. The Way will still be there.
Emergencies

is the European emergency number and it works in Spain. Say where you are as exactly as you can: the village, the stage, the last landmark you passed, and whether you are on the high road or the low road.
Check before you go

Before each mountain day, check the forecast, any local notice about the path, and the state of the high ground: snow, mist, wind. Closures and diversions change, so look at the official pages and the app, and ask where you slept.
Every reason is a reason

People come to the Primitivo for faith, for sport, for grief, for curiosity, for a rest from work, or for no reason they can name yet. This book does not rank them. The Pilgrim's Office describes the credencial as meant for those who walk with a Christian sentiment, "even if it is only with an attitude of search". You are welcome on the road whatever you bring to it, and the road does not ask you to explain.
An old road

The tradition behind this Way is old and short on certainty. Asturias tells of a king who came to see a discovery, and says in the same breath that the historical sources are not very reliable. You will walk beside ruins that remind you how long the road has been used: the sites of the old pilgrims' hospitals on the Hospitales, at Fonfaraón and Valparaíso, the half-ruined hospital at Montouto, the chapel that survives at Buspol. The Confraternity of St James records a saying that those who go to Santiago and do not visit the Saviour in Oviedo visit the servant and leave the Lord.

Asturias also says that those who know the Jacobean routes well call the Primitivo the one that has best kept the essence of the old pilgrimage, and gives the cause: a country of mountains that stayed remote and tied to the land. You do not have to believe in the essence. You can notice that the days are quiet.
What a climb gives

A long climb is a plain teacher. It sets the pace and will not be hurried, and it asks only for the next step. You may find that your thoughts slow down to match. You may find the opposite, and that a day of hard walking brings up everything you were not thinking about. Either is allowed. Wet days and mist have their own lesson, which is to attend to the ground and to the next marker.

If you walk in grief, the road holds you without asking. If you walk with doubt, walk with it. If you walk for sport, walk well, and notice who is walking beside you. If you walk with others, leave a day of the road to yourself.
Questions for the walk
Take one a day, and let it ride in your pocket. You do not have to answer.

items.t: What are you carrying that you could put down?
What did you come here to leave behind, and what did you come to find?
What would you do with this hour if you were not in a hurry?
Who do you wish were walking beside you, and what would you say to them?
What does your body need that you have been ignoring?
When did you last feel that you had enough?

spans.t: When the road is hard
Some days the climb is not a teacher. It is only a climb. On those days the kindest thing is a short plan: the next village, the next marker. Walk to that, and ask for help when you need it.
The last streets

The last descent into Santiago, past San Lázaro and through the old streets, ends at the cathedral. Wikipedia says that construction of the present building began in 1075 and that it was consecrated in 1211. It is a Romanesque church with Gothic and Baroque additions, built over the reputed tomb of St James. The Baroque façade on the Obradoiro square was completed by Fernando de Casas Novoa in 1740, and behind it the Romanesque Pórtico da Gloria of Master Mateo, carved, says Wikipedia, by 1188. The crypt below the high altar is where the pilgrims of the ninth-century church ended their journey.
Pilgrims' Masses are held in the cathedral. Their times change, so ask on the day. The
botafumeiro

, the great swinging censer, is used on certain important religious holidays and, Wikipedia says, at all Pilgrims' Masses in a Holy Year. 2027 is a Holy Year. The Holy Door is opened only in Holy Years, and the Xunta says that in a Holy Year the alternative way into the cathedral is the Holy Door at A Quintana.
The Compostela

The Compostela is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules. The Office owns the rules, and they can change. This book says what the Office says, and sends you to the Office in any doubt.

items.t: The Compostela is for those who come to the tomb of the Apostle for religious and/or spiritual reasons and follow the routes of the Way of St James on foot, by bicycle or on horseback.
It asks for at least the last hundred kilometres on foot or on horseback, or the last two hundred kilometres by bicycle, shown by the credencial, stamped along the route.

On foot or on horseback, that means at least a hundred continuous kilometres on the same route to Santiago that the Office recognises. The final stage must include at least the last one leading into the cathedral.

You may walk the Way in stages, if they follow in chronological and geographical order. A pilgrim who walks only the minimum distance must get the credencial stamped at the start and at the end of each stage, with the date.
A pilgrim who has already walked part of a recognised route outside Spain needs no less than seventy kilometres in Spain.
The Cabildo, the cathedral's governing council, reserves the right to grant the Compostela in special and exceptional cases.

spans.t: The Office awards the Compostela to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons, and it describes the pilgrimage it has in mind as one made "with a Christian sentiment, even if it is only with an attitude of search". If that does not describe your reason for walking, ask the Pilgrim's Office what it can give you: it also offers a Certificate of Distance, which records the kilometres you walked from wherever you started.

From Oviedo you have ~320 km ahead of you, far more than the last hundred kilometres the Office asks for. If your plan is anything other than walking the Way from Oviedo, or if you will walk it in stages, ask the Pilgrim's Office before you go. This book does not say whether any other start counts.
At the Pilgrim's Office

The Office issues the Compostela, a document in Latin. You will need your stamped credencial. Procedures and hours change, so look at the Office's own website before you arrive, and do not plan a tight connection for the same day.
Whatever the Compostela means to you, it is a record of a road you walked, not a measure of it.
The next day
Do not leave on the morning after you arrive. Santiago is a city built for the end of a pilgrimage, and it rewards a second day.

items.t: Rest.
After ~312 km your legs have earned it.
See the cathedral without a queue behind you.
Sit in the Obradoiro square, or at A Quintana, and watch the others arrive.
Think about what comes next.
If you want to keep walking, the Camino to Finisterre and Muxía, ~90 km, goes on from Santiago, and has its own book in this series.
Plan your way home
with the timetables in front of you, not at the last minute.

spans.t: The road ends in Santiago, and then you have to come back to a life with a ceiling and a kettle. You may find the first days strange: your legs want to walk, your pack feels missing, and the quiet of the mountains is gone. That is allowed. Give yourself a week before you decide what the walk meant.
The first days

items.t: Look after your feet and knees.
Climbs and descents leave their mark. If something still hurts after a week, see a doctor.
Wash and dry your gear
while the memory of what failed is fresh, and note what you carried and never used.
Write something down
while it is still sharp. Three lines from each region will do: the day you were tired, the day you were glad, the moment you did not expect.
Keep your credencial.
It has its own small history, now complete.

spans.t: Keeping the Way alive
You do not need a pack to keep walking. A weekly walk, however short, keeps the habit. Choose a day to walk without headphones, as you did on the road. Say
Buen Camino
to a stranger. Send a word to someone who helped you on the way.
Walking again

You have walked the Original Way, and the last ~53 km of the Camino Francés with it. If you want more, the Camino Francés (~773 km) has its own book in this series, and so does the Camino del Norte (~820 km), which, Wikipedia says, also joins the Francés at Arzúa. The Camino Inglés (~120 km) is short, and has a book too. A road does not have to be longer or harder to be worth walking. It only has to be yours.
Buen Camino
, and good to have you home.
With the CaminoPlus app
CaminoPlus
is the offline-first companion app for the Camino de Santiago, with maps that work without signal, stays and cafes, a pilgrim passport with stamps, a journal and friends. The paid plan is called
Pilgrim Plus

. The app is still in development. The Camino Primitivo is on its list of routes, but this book makes no claim about what the app holds for it today, so look in the app, and use it, not this book, for beds, cafes, closures and weather.

A reminder about the passport: the Pilgrim's Office asks for the stamped credencial. A passport in CaminoPlus, or in any app other than the Office's own digital credential, is a keepsake until the Office says otherwise.
Sources and thanks
This book rests on public sources, and its fact ledger lists every fact against the page it came from. The chief ones are:

items.t: The Principado de Asturias tourism pages
(turismoasturias.es): the pages on the Camino Primitivo and its seven stages through Asturias, the practical information for pilgrims, the page on gastronomy, and the official Camino brochure.
The Xunta de Galicia

, on its official Camino de Santiago portal (caminodesantiago.gal): the Primitive Way page and its Galician stages, with their lengths, sections and descriptions, and the Melide to Arzúa stage of the French Way.
The Pilgrim's Reception Office of the Cathedral of Santiago
(oficinadelperegrino.com): the rules of the Compostela, the credencial and the history of the pilgrimage.
The Confraternity of St James
(csj.org.uk): its page on the Camino Primitivo.
Wikipedia

, for history, geography, climate tables and the Pilgrim's Office statistics for 2024: the articles on the Camino Primitivo, Oviedo, Lugo, A Fonsagrada, Melide, Arzúa, Santiago de Compostela and its cathedral, Santiago airport, the Jacobean Holy Year, Galicia, Asturias, and three dishes; and the Spanish Wikipedia's article on the Ruta Jacobea Primitiva, for its kilometre table and its account of the Hospitales variant.
A standard solar calculation
, for the hours of daylight at Oviedo and Lugo.

spans.t: Published figures differ between these sources, so every distance in this book is marked ~. Where the sources say nothing, for example on a closing date for the high variant, the book says nothing and tells you to check. If you know a better figure, or a fact that has changed, tell CaminoPlus.
Thanks go to the people who keep the Way: the associations of friends of the Camino, the hosts who open the hostels, and the people in the villages and towns who point the way and say
Buen Camino
to a stranger.
A short glossary

items.t: Albergue
: a pilgrims' hostel with shared rooms.
Botafumeiro
: the great censer of Santiago cathedral.
Buen Camino
: "good Way", the greeting between pilgrims.
Cabildo
: the governing council of the cathedral.
Compostela
: the Latin certificate the Pilgrim's Office issues.
Credencial
: the pilgrim's passport.
Hórreo
: a raised granary, a mark of the Asturian countryside.
Hospitales
: the high variant of the Camino Primitivo, named for its ruined pilgrims' hospitals.
Hospitalero
: the host of a pilgrims' hostel.
Menú del peregrino
: a set meal for pilgrims.
Palloza
: a primitive rural dwelling of the mountains.
Sello
: a stamp in the credencial.
